To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Peritoneal cells, in a culture system that permits their growth as a monolayer, form antibody to sheep erythrocytes and that this antibody can be detected by a plaque-forming cell assay.

(1) PC from unimmunized, normal, adult female mice, but not from young male mice or mice of either sex that had been immunized with SRBC 4-6 days earlier, could form plaques of lyses of SRBC in monolayer microcultures containing CMC and complement; (2) the plaque-forming capacity was dependent on an optimum cell concentration, and was inhibited at supraoptimal and suboptimal cell densities; (3) the plaque

(i) PC from young, unimmunised male mice are the most effective of the various cell sources tested in the plaque assay; (ii) the plaque assay is dependent on cell concentration, with optimal plaque counts at about 5 x 10 6/ml; (iii) the plaque assay can be specifically and reversably suppressed by anti-IgM serum, but not by anti-IgG; (iv) the plaque assay of PC can be specifically and irreversibly suppressed
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the cell types that form plaques in our microcultures.
the study of the mechanism of antibody formation in vitro by peritoneal macrophages from unimmunized animals.
the in vitro stimulation of the antibody forming capacity of mouse peritoneal cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the in vitro stimulation of antibody formation by PC from normal mice is a process that is sensitive to metabolic inhibitors, is dependent on cell to cell interaction, and is probably mediated by IgM.

PC from normal, unstimulated mice can produce plaques of lyses of SRBC in CMC microculturing, that this plaque formation is specific and dependent on an interaction between PC, that it is due to the production of IgM antibody by these cells, and that the plaque formation is inhibited by metabolic inhibitors.
PC from normal mice are able to produce hemolytic IgM antibodies to SRBC when stimulated by SRBC in vitro in a microculture system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PFC compartment of PC is a dynamic one in which there is an equilibrium between cells in various stages of differentiation.
PC are capable of synthesizing antibody to SRBC, and that this synthesis is subject to control at the genetic level, as well as to nutritional and other nonspecific factors.
the in vitro plaque-forming cell is not a single cell, but a population of cells, some of which are sensitive to inhibitors of DNA and protein synthesis and others which are resistant.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the in vivo and in vitro stimulation of PFC by peritoneal macrophages can be studied by the use of the plaque assay in microcultures, and that this assay is more sensitive than the usual macroculture plaque assay, which is not suitable for the study of peritoneal cells.
the PC compartment is a heterogeneous one, and the PFC are not a uniform population.
the PC of the mouse can be induced to make antibody, and that the process can be studied in vitro.
